passages.happening:
Paul says he could not speak to the Corinthians as spiritual people. He had to speak to them “as infants in Christ” (verse 1).

“I gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for solid food” (verse 2). Then the sting: “In fact, you are still not ready” (verse 2).

The reason is plain. “For since there is jealousy and dissension among you, are you not worldly? Are you not walking in the way of man?” (verse 3).

He names the evidence: “For when one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ and another, ‘I follow Apollos,’ are you not mere men?” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 2 Paul described the spiritual person, taught by God's Spirit. The Corinthians would have been glad to hear it. They thought of themselves that way. Now Paul turns the description into a mirror.

‘Worldly’ translates two related Greek words. In verse 1 it is sarkinos, made of flesh: simply young and not yet grown. In verse 3 it is sarkikos, ruled by the flesh, living by merely human ways. The Corinthians had begun as babies, which is no shame. The shame is that years later they still acted like it.

Milk and solid food are a picture of lessons for beginners and lessons for the grown-up. Paul does not mean he kept back a secret teaching. The ‘milk’ and the ‘solid food’ are the same Christ crucified. What changes is how deeply a person can take it in.

What is Paul's test of maturity? Not how much they know, how well they speak, or what gifts they have. The Corinthians had plenty of all three. His test is how they treat one another. Jealousy and quarrels prove they are still infants.

‘Walking in the way of man’ means living as anyone in Corinth lived: competing for status, taking sides, looking for a famous name to attach yourself to.
passages.ot:
The picture of God's people as children who must be fed and taught runs through the Old Testament. Through Hosea God says of Israel, “When Israel was a child, I loved him” (Hosea 11:1), and “It was I who taught Ephraim to walk” (Hosea 11:3).

Other New Testament writers use the same picture of milk. The letter to the Hebrews says, “You need milk, not solid food” (Hebrews 5:12). Peter tells new believers, “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation” (1 Peter 2:2). Milk is not bad. Staying on it forever is.

The warning against jealousy and strife echoes the wisdom of Proverbs: “Be not wise in your own eyes” (Proverbs 3:7).
passages.asks: Paul measures growth by love, not by knowledge. Ask what you use as the measure of a mature Christian. Then ask where jealousy or taking sides shows up in you. That is the place, Paul would say, where you are still an infant, and where God wants you to grow.

passages.t: Planting and watering: God gives the growth
passages.happening:
“What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role” (verse 5).

Paul uses a picture from the farm. “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (verse 6). So the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing; only God, who makes things grow, matters (verse 7).

The planter and the waterer are “one in purpose” (verse 8). Each will be rewarded for his own work.

“For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
‘Servants’ here is the Greek diakonoi, people who serve others: a word used for those who waited at table. Paul does not ask, ‘Who is Apollos?’ but ‘What is Apollos?’ He is a tool in God's hand, not a name to rally behind.

Most people in the Roman world lived from the land, and even city people knew how a crop grows. One worker sows and another waters, but no worker can make a seed sprout. The hearers could picture it at once.

The order of Paul's words matters. He and Apollos are ‘God's fellow workers’, working alongside one another for God. The church is ‘God's field’ and ‘God's building’. The word ‘God's’ comes first each time in the Greek. The church does not belong to its planter or to its waterer. It belongs to God.

Each worker will receive his own reward, Paul says. That answers a Corinthian worry. If the church stops ranking leaders, will good work go unnoticed? No. God sees it, and God will reward it. The church does not need to hand out praise like a city honouring its benefactors.

‘Building’ in verse 9 prepares for the next picture. Paul turns from the field to the builder's yard.
passages.ot:
Israel is often pictured as God's planting. Isaiah sings of God's vineyard: “He dug it up and cleared the stones and planted the finest vines” (Isaiah 5:2). Through Isaiah God promised that his people would be called “oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD” (Isaiah 61:3).

God gave Jeremiah a calling in the same two pictures Paul uses, farming and building: “to build and plant” (Jeremiah 1:10).

And a psalm says what Paul says about the builder: “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1).
passages.asks: If you serve in a church in any way, ask whether you are planting and watering for God or building a name for yourself. If you belong to a church, ask whether you give its leaders more honour than God. Paul's words free leaders from carrying what only God can do, and they free churches from making idols of leaders.

passages.t: The one foundation, and the testing fire
passages.happening:
Paul now speaks as a builder. “By the grace God has given me, I laid a foundation as an expert builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one must be careful how he builds” (verse 10).

There is only one foundation: “For no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (verse 11).

People build on it with different materials: gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay or straw (verse 12). One day each builder's work will be shown for what it is. “his workmanship will be evident, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work” (verse 13).

If what he built survives, he will be rewarded (verse 14). “If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
‘Expert builder’ is the Greek architektōn, from which English gets architect. It meant the master builder who oversaw the whole work. Paul laid the foundation when he first preached Christ in Corinth. Others, such as Apollos and the teachers who followed, built on it.

Corinth was a city of building. After it was founded again as a Roman colony, temples, markets and colonnades rose, many paid for by wealthy citizens. Fine stone buildings stood near houses of wood with thatched roofs. And fire was a real danger in an ancient city. Everyone knew what fire did to wood and straw, and what it could not do to stone and metal.

The materials are a picture. Gold, silver and precious stones stand for work that lasts. Wood, hay and straw stand for work that looks fine for now and will not survive. Paul does not say exactly what each material means. In this chapter the most likely sense is the quality of teaching and leadership: work that builds people up on Christ, or work that builds on cleverness, status and party spirit.

‘The Day’ is the day of the Lord, when Christ comes as judge. Paul spoke of it in 1:8. On that day all work will be shown for what it is.

Notice who is being tested. In this passage it is first the builders: those who teach and lead the church. Paul is warning the Corinthians' favourite teachers, and himself.
passages.ot:
The one foundation recalls Isaiah, where God says, “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation” (Isaiah 28:16). The first Christians read that stone as Christ.

Fire that tests and purifies is an Old Testament picture of God's judgment. Malachi asks, “But who can endure the day of His coming?” and answers, “For He will be like a refiner’s fire” (Malachi 3:2). Through Zechariah God says, “I will refine them like silver and test them like gold” (Zechariah 13:9). Paul uses the same picture: a fire that shows what is precious and burns what is not.

Gold, silver and precious stones were among the materials David gathered for the temple: “gold for the gold articles, silver for the silver” and “all kinds of precious stones” (1 Chronicles 29:2). That prepares for what Paul says next: the building is a temple.
passages.hard:
“He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames” (verse 15). What does this fire mean? Christians have read this verse in two main ways. Each is set out here as its own holders would put it. These notes take no side.

The Catholic Church teaches a doctrine called purgatory: a final purification, after death, of those who die in God's grace and friendship but are not yet fully purified. They are sure of salvation, and they are made ready for the holiness of heaven. The Catechism of the Catholic Church speaks of this as a cleansing fire and points to this verse, together with 1 Peter 1:7, among the passages behind the teaching. Catholics read it as showing that a person can be saved and yet pass through a purifying fire. They also point to the ancient practice of praying for the dead.

Protestant churches do not teach purgatory. They read the verse in its setting, about builders, especially teachers and leaders, whose work will be tested on the Day of judgment. On this reading the fire tests the work, not the person. A minister whose work proves worthless will lose his reward, but not his salvation, because he stands on the foundation, Christ. He will be saved ‘as if through the flames’, like a man who escapes a burning house with nothing left. Protestants hold that Christ's death has fully dealt with the believer's sin, so no further cleansing after death is needed.

Both readings agree on a good deal. The verse speaks of a real judgment of what believers have done. A person can be saved while much of their work proves worthless. And the foundation is Christ, not the builder. That is a comfort and a warning at once.

Verse 17 is sterner: “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him” (verse 17). Readers differ on whether that warns believers who tear the church apart, or those outside who attack it.
passages.asks: Paul asks every builder to be careful how he builds. Ask what you are building your life, your family or your work in the church with: things that will last, or things that only look good now. Ask whether Christ is truly the foundation, or whether something else is quietly carrying the weight.

passages.happening:
“Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (verse 16).

Then a warning: “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
In English ‘you’ can mean one person or many. In Greek the two are different. Here every ‘you’ is plural. Paul is not yet speaking of each believer's body as a temple; he will say that in 6:19. Here he means the church together. The whole gathered church in Corinth is God's temple.

The word is naos, the inner shrine of a temple, the room where the god was thought to live. Corinth had many temples, to Apollo, Aphrodite, the healing god Asclepius and others. Each had its shrine and its image. For Jews there was one temple, in Jerusalem, where God had put his name and his presence.

So Paul's claim is astonishing. A small, quarrelling group of ordinary people, meeting in a house, with no building at all, is the place where God's Spirit lives. Not a statue. Not a shrine. A people.

That makes division serious. To split the church into parties is not a matter of taste. It is damaging the house God lives in. ‘God's temple is holy’, and Paul says the Corinthians are that temple.
passages.ot:
God's desire to live among his people runs through the whole Old Testament. At Sinai God said, “Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God” (Exodus 29:45). In the law he promised, “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:12). Ezekiel looked ahead to a day when God's dwelling place would be with them (Ezekiel 37:27).

Solomon, at the dedication of the temple, knew no building could hold God: “Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built” (1 Kings 8:27). Paul says God now dwells, by his Spirit, in a people.

Jesus had spoken of his own body as the temple: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again” (John 2:19).
passages.asks: If your church is the place where God's Spirit lives, ask how you speak about it and to it. Gossip, contempt and taking sides are not small things in God's house. Ask whether there is a division you have fed, and what it would mean to stop.

passages.happening:
“Let no one deceive himself. If any of you thinks he is wise in this age, he should become a fool, so that he may become wise” (verse 18).

“For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight” (verse 19). Paul quotes Scripture twice: God “catches the wise in their craftiness” (verse 19), and “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile” (verse 20).

So, Paul says, “stop boasting in men. All things are yours” (verse 21). He lists them: “whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future. All of them belong to you” (verse 22).

Then the last line turns the order around: “and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The Corinthians had been saying, ‘I follow Paul’, ‘I follow Apollos’, as if they belonged to a leader. Paul turns their slogans upside down. You do not belong to Paul. Paul belongs to you. So does Apollos, and Cephas. All of them are gifts God has given the church. Why choose one gift and refuse the others?

Then the list grows beyond leaders to everything: the world, life, death, the present and the future. In a city where people feared fate, and where death was the end of every ambition, Paul says even death belongs to the believer. It cannot own them.

But the chain does not stop with them. ‘You belong to Christ.’ The Corinthians are not owners at the top of the ladder. They are owned, bought and held by Christ. The freedom of ‘all things are yours’ rests on belonging to someone.

‘Christ belongs to God’ does not mean Christ is less than God. Paul confesses Jesus as the one Lord through whom all things came (8:6). He is speaking of the Son who came from the Father and does the Father's will. The order runs all the way up to God, and all the way down to the gifts the church receives.

‘Become a fool’ means being willing to look foolish by the world's measure, by trusting a crucified Lord, in order to be truly wise.
passages.ot:
Paul quotes two Old Testament passages. The first is Job 5:13: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (Job 5:13). The words are spoken by Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, to whom God says at the end, “you have not spoken about Me accurately” (Job 42:7). But this line is true in itself, and Paul uses it as Scripture: God cannot be outwitted by clever people.

The second is Psalm 94:11. In the Berean Standard Bible the psalm reads, “The LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are futile” (Psalm 94:11). Paul has ‘the thoughts of the wise’. He seems to apply the psalm's word ‘man’ to the people he is speaking about, those who think themselves wise. The psalm is about proud people who think God does not see. God knows their thoughts, and they come to nothing.

Paul's list of ‘life or death or the present or the future’ is close to his great list in Romans: “neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future” (Romans 8:38).
passages.asks: Ask which teachers or traditions you have treated as the only ones worth hearing. Paul says they all belong to you: you can learn from many. Then ask the harder question: do you belong to Christ? Everything else is held by that.
